entries.title: Uncovering the Mechanisms of Policy Interventions: A Difference-In-Differences Framework for Mediation Analysis
entries.summary: The paper develops a two-period difference-in-differences mediation framework that relaxes the usual sequential ignorability requirement by relying on change-based assumptions. It also extends the approach to staggered adoption and provides an open-source R package.
entries.why_it_matters: This gives people analytics teams a clearer way to test whether interventions such as training, policy changes, or staffing changes work through a proposed mechanism when pre-existing differences may confound levels. It is especially useful for evaluation designs that have pre/post data but cannot defend a standard cross-sectional mediation model.

entries.title: A Psychometric Evaluation of Single-Item Measures
entries.summary: The manuscript reviews when single-item measures can and cannot support claims about reliability and validity, using classical test theory, item response theory, and generalizability theory. It argues that single-item measures cannot demonstrate latent factor structure or internal consistency, but can still be appropriate for some kinds of reliability and validity evidence.
entries.why_it_matters: This can inform survey design when you need ultra-short measures for pulse checks, repeated surveys, or respondent-burden constraints. It also cautions analysts against treating a single item like a full multi-item scale when interpreting people data.

entries.title: The Organizational Benefits of Neurodiversity: A Strategic Human Capital–Based Systematic Review and Research Agenda
entries.summary: The review synthesizes 88 studies on HRM and neurodiversity and finds that the literature is growing but organizational-level evidence is still limited and uneven. It proposes a research agenda focused on how neurodivergent human capital may create organizational value and through what processes.
entries.why_it_matters: This can guide inclusion, accommodation, and talent strategy decisions by separating ethical inclusion goals from measurable business outcomes. It also shows where evidence is thin, which helps when choosing evaluation metrics or building an internal case for neurodiversity initiatives.

entries.title: Job Demands-Resources, Well-Being and Work-Life Boundaries: The Pervasiveness of Social Networking Platforms
entries.summary: Based on qualitative interviews with 67 managers, the paper links work-oriented social networking to job demands, resources, boundary blurring, and well-being through an integrated job demands-resources and boundary-theory lens. It identifies professional-personal, accessibility-inaccessibility, and control-autonomy boundary tensions.
entries.why_it_matters: This can inform policy choices about after-hours messaging, platform norms, and manager training on boundary management. It is useful for diagnosing why a collaboration tool may function as a resource in one context and a demand in another.

entries.title: How Can Talent Managers Create Organizational Value Throughout the Hype Cycles of Emerging and Innovative Industries?
entries.summary: Using interviews with 14 experienced executives plus industry and media evidence, the paper argues that talent management systems in emerging industries need to shift across hype-cycle phases rather than stay fixed. It frames value creation as contingent on changing legitimacy, regulation, expectations, and resource availability.
entries.why_it_matters: This can help HR and talent leaders in emerging sectors decide when to emphasize hiring, retention, capability building, or restructuring as industry conditions change. It is useful for scenario planning and for aligning talent architecture to market maturity rather than copying a generic best-practice bundle.
